extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and counsel involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings and petitions for reconsideration (attorneys practicing before the USPTO, OED counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria governing requests for reconsideration, reopening, record corrections, waiver petitions, and related procedural/legal showings in USPTO disciplinary matters under 37 C.F.R. Part 11. Focuses on § 11.56(c) reconsideration, § 11.55 reopening, corporate-officer practice authorization, and related authority (Sperry, Kroll, TMEP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration under 37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following a final decision of the USPTO Director, either party may make a single request for reconsideration or modification if filed within twenty days from the date of entry of the decision and the request is based on newly discovered evidence, or an error of law or fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests under § 11.56(c) must show that (a) the ground is newly discovered evidence or an error of law or fact, and (b) any newly discovered evidence could not have been discovered earlier by due diligence. The standard of review is very high; such motions are extraordinary and should be granted sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow standard of review (analogous to Fed. R. Civ. P. 59/60)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriate standard for § 11.56(c) is narrow and limited, analogous to motions to alter or amend a judgment under Federal Rules 59(e) and 60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts grant relief under these rules only in certain limited circumstances (e.g., newly discovered evidence, correcting errors of law or fact). Reconsideration is not an avenue for reargument or dissatisfaction with the outcome. Examples where reconsideration might be appropriate include a court's patent misunderstanding of a party, decision outside the adversarial issues, or an error of apprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newly discovered evidence — availability and due diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence is not "newly discovered" if it was available to the party prior to entry of judgment; the requester must demonstrate that the evidence could not have been discovered earlier by due diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits or documents that clarify previously available deposition testimony or that are substantially similar to record material will not satisfy the standard. Courts reject affidavits that could have been produced earlier given opportunity (citations: Boryan v. United States; Fredericks v. Wyle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration is not for relitigation or mere disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for reconsideration may not be used to relitigate old matters, rehash arguments previously presented, or state mere disagreement with a final judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere repetition of prior arguments or filing additional arguments/evidence that could have been raised earlier is improper. Decisions cite that an unhappy litigant may not obtain one more chance to sway the adjudicator (Hutchinson; Above the Belt; Arthur v. King).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary remedy requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconsideration motions are extraordinary remedies reserved for extraordinary circumstances and should be used sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relief under the analogous federal rules (e.g., Rule 60(b)(6)) is limited to extraordinary circumstances; similarly, § 11.56(c) relief is rare and requires strong justification (Dowell v. State Farm; Projects Mgmt. v. DynCorp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial similarity to the record defeats "new" evidence claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that is substantially similar to material already in the administrative record does not qualify as newly discovered evidence under § 11.56(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If deposition testimony or other record evidence already conveys the same facts, a later-submitted affidavit repeating those facts will not meet the standard. Reconsideration is denied where the new submission adds no materially new information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests to reopen disciplinary proceeding under 37 C.F.R. § 11.55(h)
rubrics_metrics.description: A request to reopen a disciplinary proceeding on the basis of newly discovered evidence must demonstrate that the newly discovered evidence could not have been discovered by due diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.55(h)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reopening requires documentary support and legal analysis showing why the evidence is new and why reopening is justified; vague assertions or untimely material are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting the administrative record — completeness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A request to correct or augment the administrative record must supply justification and legal authority demonstrating that the record is incomplete and that omitted materials should be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Director's prior determination that the Administrative Record is complete will not be reversed absent new justification; mere allegations that records were 'lost' without substantiation are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate-officer authorization under 37 C.F.R. § 11.14(e)(3) is fact-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that a practitioner acted as a designated corporate officer (and thus was authorized to file) requires evidence that the practitioner in fact acted in that corporate capacity; mere designation or later claim does not automatically legitimize filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP guidance (e.g., §§ 611.02, 611.06(d)) may interpret § 11.14(e)(3), but a party alleging corporate-officer practice must demonstrate through record evidence that filings were made in the officer role; an asserted automatic cloak of authority without supporting legal authority is rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Briefing requirements — adequate presentation of standard of review and legal analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal brief must adequately present the applicable standard of review and provide sufficient legal analysis demonstrating errors committed by the ALJ or decision-maker; meeting only literal citation requirements (e.g., listing authorities) is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truncated one-sentence legal assertions or lack of citations to record or authority, when they fail to demonstrate substantive analysis or identify errors, can justify refusal to accept or to consider portions of a brief (see USPTO orders refusing entry of inadequate briefs). Reliance on the 'whole record' does not excuse the need to show why the record demonstrates error.

rubrics_metrics.name: State bar discipline is not dispositive for USPTO disciplinary decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A state bar's choice not to discipline an individual is irrelevant to USPTO disciplinary proceedings; regulation of practice before the USPTO is within the Office's exclusive authority (Sperry; Kroll).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that state bars did not act do not demonstrate error of law or fact by the USPTO Director and do not satisfy reconsideration standards. USPTO discipline is governed by federal authority over admission and practice before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver and suspension of rules — correct statutory/regulatory provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions to waive regulations must invoke the correct provision: § 1.183 applies only to Part 1 regulations (patent practice); Part 11 regulations (practitioners) are not waivable under § 1.183; petitions to waive Part 11 rules must identify the regulation and show extraordinary circumstances under § 11.3 if applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing a nonexistent or inapplicable waiver provision is fatal. For disciplinary/regulatory waivers in Part 11, the petitioner must identify the specific regulations to be waived and demonstrate the extraordinary situation required by § 11.3; unsupported claims of innocence or political motivation are insufficient.
